elements.element: Customer has no minimum purchase or volume commitment.
elements.evidence: Section 2.1 expressly commits Customer to purchase at least USD 2,000,000 during the current twelve-month term. Section 12.3's contrary acknowledgement does not eliminate that express obligation and instead creates an operative conflict.

elements.element: Customer pays fees only for actual usage or Services ordered.
elements.evidence: Section 2.1 requires a true-up for the difference between the commitment and Fees for Services ordered, so Customer may owe amounts beyond usage or ordered Services.

elements.element: Any minimum purchase commitment is limited to the current twelve-month term.
elements.evidence: Section 2.1 states that the commitment applies during the current twelve-month term only and does not apply to a subsequent term absent a new written agreement.

elements.element: Customer may reduce the commitment on 30 days' notice.
elements.evidence: Section 2.1 expressly permits Customer to reduce the commitment on 30 days' written notice.

elements.element: Any shortfall is resolved solely through a true-up calculated against the committed amount as reduced.
elements.evidence: Section 2.1 makes Customer's sole shortfall obligation a true-up equal to the difference between the committed amount, as reduced, and Fees for Services ordered.

elements.element: No penalty applies for a shortfall.
elements.evidence: Section 2.1 expressly excludes penalties, liquidated damages, and accelerated Fees.

result.reason: The redline substantively reaches the fallback but not the preferred position. It is not strictly minimal because it adds an express termination right beyond the stated reduction right. More importantly, it leaves Section 12.3's acknowledgement that Customer made no minimum-volume commitment directly inconsistent with Section 2.1's USD 2,000,000 commitment. That unresolved operative contradiction reduces certainty and drafting quality even though Section 2.1 contains each fallback protection.
